Point-in-polygon analysis

Load the following packages:

Now load simple feature files of Marine Protected Areas in Indonesia and do a standard point-in-polygon analysis.

indo.marine <- st_read("indo.marine.gpkg")
## Reading layer `indo.marine' from data source 
##   `/Users/qadirqueen/Desktop/ECON 425 R Day Files/indo.marine.gpkg' 
##   using driver `GPKG'
## Simple feature collection with 102 features and 32 fields
## Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
## Dimension:     XY
## Bounding box:  xmin: 95.31916 ymin: -11.15609 xmax: 136.7428 ymax: 5.91849
## Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84

Make a subset of some of the biggest protected areas in order to map them:

indo.marine.big <- subset(indo.marine,indo.marine$GIS_M_AREA>2e+03)

load data on fishing boats detected using SAR (synthetic aperture radar) for the month of May 2025:

sar_data <- read_csv("sar_vessel_detections_pipev3_202505.csv")
## Rows: 213368 Columns: 10
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## chr (3): scene_id, timestamp, matched_category
## dbl (7): lat, lon, presence_score, length_m, mmsi, matching_score, fishing_s...
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

This is a lot of data so let’s just keep boats near Indonesia and with a “fishing score” greater than 0.5. This means a machine learning model thinks the boat is likely to be a fishing boat. And let’s also turn this dataset into a Special Features file so we can do spatial analysis.

indonesia.fishing.boats <- subset(sar_data, sar_data$lat<8 & sar_data$lat> -14 & sar_data$lon < 142 & sar_data$lon > 92 & sar_data$fishing_score>0.5 )
indonesia.fishing.boats_sf <- st_as_sf(indonesia.fishing.boats, coords = c('lon', 'lat'), crs = 4326)

Let’s make a map of a few of these MPAs and the detected fishing boat locations (it takes a really long time to map all 100 MPAs because of the detail involved):

theme_set(theme_bw())
ggplot() +
    coord_quickmap() + 
    geom_sf(data = indonesia.fishing.boats_sf) +
  geom_point(data = indonesia.fishing.boats, aes(x = lon, y = lat),size=0.1, col="red") + 
  geom_sf(data = subset(indo.marine.big,indo.marine.big$WDPAID==8102), fill=NA, col="darkblue") +
  geom_sf(data = subset(indo.marine.big,indo.marine.big$WDPAID==555511970), fill=NA, col="darkblue") +
  geom_sf(data = subset(indo.marine.big,indo.marine.big$WDPAID==198427), fill=NA, col="darkblue") +
  geom_sf(data = subset(indo.marine.big,indo.marine.big$WDPAID==555511989), fill=NA, col="darkblue") +
  geom_sf(data = subset(indo.marine.big,indo.marine.big$WDPAID==555635921), fill=NA, col="darkblue") +
   geom_sf(data = subset(indo.marine.big,indo.marine.big$WDPAID==8871), fill=NA, col="darkblue") +
   geom_sf(data = subset(indo.marine.big,indo.marine.big$WDPAID== 555511958), fill=NA, col="darkblue") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(92, 142), ylim = c(-14, 8), expand = FALSE)  + 
  xlab("Longitude") + ylab("Latitude")
## Coordinate system already present.
## ℹ Adding new coordinate system, which will replace the existing one.

Now let’s count how many boats (red dots) are inside each Marine Protected Area (dark blue polygons):

indo.marine <- indo.marine %>%
  mutate(pt_count = lengths(st_intersects(indo.marine, indonesia.fishing.boats_sf)))

Regression analysis

Create a variable for whether an MPA is strictly enforced based on the IUCN categories:

indo.marine$strict.protection <- ifelse(indo.marine$IUCN_CAT=="Ia" | indo.marine$IUCN_CAT=="II" | indo.marine$IUCN_CAT=="III",1,0)

Run a regression where the number of boats detected in each MPA is our y or outcome variable and our x or explanatory variables are the size of the MPA measured using GIS (GIS_M_AREA), the year the MPA was established as a sign of how old it is (STATUS_YR), and our strict protection measure:

may2025.lm <- lm(pt_count ~ GIS_M_AREA + STATUS_YR + strict.protection, data=indo.marine)
summary(may2025.lm)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = pt_count ~ GIS_M_AREA + STATUS_YR + strict.protection, 
##     data = indo.marine)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -19.281  -2.290  -1.272   0.259  34.063 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                     Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)        4.0587047  1.6800014   2.416   0.0175 *  
## GIS_M_AREA         0.0009729  0.0001673   5.814 7.62e-08 ***
## STATUS_YR         -0.0014282  0.0009047  -1.579   0.1176    
## strict.protection -4.5320147  2.1970832  -2.063   0.0418 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
##

## Multiple R-squared:  0.2581, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2354 
## F-statistic: 11.37 on 3 and 98 DF,  p-value: 1.841e-06

Conclusion

Based on these results, we can conclude the following:

  • Bigger marine protected areas have more illegal fishing (99% confident)

  • Older protected areas have less illegal fishing (93% confident)

  • Strictly protected areas have less illegal fishing (94% confident)

These conclusions all make sense: (i) the larger the area, the harder it is to enforce, (ii) areas that have been established for a long time probably have greater public awareness and (iii) strictly protected areas tend to have better enforcement and less loopholes that allow some fishing to take place.
